transcript.speaker: skeptic
transcript.content:
The accountability gap in this resolution is real, documented, and ugly. Workers get fired by hiring algorithms they never see. Families get denied mortgages by credit models nobody can explain. The Federal Trade Commission and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission have both warned since 2021 that automated systems produce discriminatory outcomes their victims cannot trace. So I will not pretend the problem is invented. The disease is concentrated corporate power and information asymmetry. The disease is not a shortage of audit logs.

Here is where the resolution breaks. A cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened. It does not prove why. Provenance is not interpretability. You can put a flawless chain-of-custody stamp on a black box and still have no idea what the box did or why it denied someone a loan. Deep-learning systems generate decisions through millions of weighted parameters that resist human-readable explanation. Logging the output of an unexplainable system does not make it explainable. It makes it timestamped. Companies already turn narrow third-party audits into deflection instruments, and a federal logging mandate hands them a new one.

Now translate the discovery half into a courtroom. Congress expands discovery rights tomorrow. A fired warehouse worker gets the cryptographic logs. They still need an expert who can reverse-engineer a proprietary model to prove the firing was discriminatory. That expertise costs money the plaintiff does not have. And the vendor's licensing agreement still bars independent inspection of the source model under trade-secret protection. Procedural access without interpretive capacity reproduces the exact asymmetry it claims to close. The defendant has the engineers. The plaintiff has a hard drive full of encrypted records and no way to read them.

The phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is doing dishonest work. Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act already prohibit discriminatory outcomes regardless of intent or cause. Disparate-impact doctrine does not require you to crack open the algorithm. It requires you to show the result lands harder on a protected class. That is a result you can measure from the outside, without subject-keyed logs. The real threat to accountability is not a missing logging standard. It is the active federal effort to gut disparate-impact liability itself. Whoever wins that fight decides whether existing law has teeth. A new cryptographic architecture does nothing if the underlying right is being dismantled in parallel.

Ask one more question before Congress builds anything. Whoever writes the audit-trail standard and controls the keys controls accountability. That is an infrastructure project with a chokepoint, and the firms best positioned to write the standard are the same incumbents the mandate is supposed to constrain. So before we mandate millions of encrypted records nobody can interpret, I want the proponents to name one deployed audit-trail mandate, anywhere, where a victim used the logs to prove not that a decision occurred, but why. If that case does not exist, what exactly are we building?

The core compliance-theater critique ('logging the output of an unexplainable system makes it timestamped, not explainable') is built directly on this node's VULNERABLE flag: mandatory disclosure produces voluminous low-signal artifacts that obscure decision logic, especially for emergent neural-network behavior. The statement self-monitors the technocratic-solutionism trap by distinguishing provenance from interpretability.

The third paragraph's courtroom walkthrough — the fired worker who gets cryptographic logs but still cannot afford an expert to reverse-engineer a proprietary model — is a concrete dramatization of this belief that victims lack the technical knowledge to prove causation. It grounds the claim that procedural access without interpretive capacity reproduces asymmetry.

The fourth paragraph's challenge to 'fundamentally incapable' — Title VII, Fair Housing Act, ADA already reach discriminatory outcomes via disparate-impact doctrine — draws on this node's VULNERABLE note that existing civil rights statutes may make AI-specific architecture duplicative. The statement also imports the watchlist caveat by naming sit-169 (federal dismantling of disparate-impact liability) as the real fight rather than naively assuming enforcement is frictionless.

The argument that vendor licensing agreements bar independent inspection of the source model under trade-secret protection — even after logs are mandated — comes directly from this belief, reinforcing that contractual barriers persist alongside any new disclosure regime.

policy_refs.relevance: The statement implicitly favors investment in interpretability research over cryptographic logging, since its central distinction (provenance is not interpretability) implies that understanding model internals — not timestamping outputs — is what closes the accountability gap.

The argument is skeptical of this transparency-mandate-style policy as applied through cryptographic audit trails, warning that disclosure mandates can become compliance theater that satisfies the letter without enabling causation proof or remediation.

transcript.speaker: safetyist
transcript.content:
The Skeptic has made the strongest argument in this room, and it deserves to be stated plainly: a cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened, but it does not prove why it happened. Provenance is not interpretability. Log a black box, and you get tamper-proof opacity — a timestamp on a decision no one can explain. The Skeptic is right that existing law already reaches discriminatory outcomes from the outside: Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the ADA let plaintiffs prove disparate impact without ever reading a model's weights. That doctrine works, and the real threat to it is the 2025 federal effort to gut disparate-impact liability, not a missing audit standard.

Here is where my evidence leads somewhere else. The resolution's phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is an overstatement, and the Skeptic's defense of existing doctrine is a floor — but a floor is not a deterrent. Tort liability cannot reliably deter diffuse, probabilistic, multi-causal harm, where a single denied loan or flagged résumé is one of ten million outputs. Product-safety law solved this exact problem in 1963, when California adopted strict product liability in Greenman v. Yuba Power: the manufacturer answers for the defective product regardless of fault, because proving negligence in a complex system is hopeless. Accountability cannot be automated. It terminates in a named human fiduciary who answers for the system, or it terminates nowhere.

So I concede the Skeptic's central point and convert it. The audit trail is not the remedy — it is one structural beam. It records the WHAT. Interpretability records the WHY. The named fiduciary is the load-bearing column: the WHO answers. Mandate the log alone, and you build compliance theater — the same deflection that let third-party algorithmic audits in 2021 certify systems no plaintiff could ever read. The FTC and EEOC warned that year that algorithmic discrimination was already actionable, yet warnings without an interpretable record and a liable person produce paper, not deterrence. Subject-keyed logs without a parallel interpretability mandate timestamp opacity. That is the gap the resolution leaves open.

The chokepoint objection is the one I will own rather than dodge, because it is correct and it is unsolved. Whoever writes the audit standard and holds the keys controls accountability. No deployed mandate anywhere has yet demonstrated capture-resistant key custody — there is no clean affirmative precedent, and I will not invent one. Concentrating key control creates its own failure mode: incumbent lock-in, where the three or four firms large enough to write the standard capture it. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer. The lesson is not that oversight fails — it is that delegated certification fails. Independent custody and transparent criteria are preconditions for this mechanism, not afterthoughts.

What would have to be true for both the Skeptic and the resolution to hold? Existing law would have to be simultaneously sufficient and nonexistent. It is neither. It is a floor under active dismantling, and a floor that never deterred the diffuse harm in the first place. The disagreement is not audit-trail versus nothing. It is whether Congress builds one beam and calls it a structure, or builds the load-bearing column — the strict liability and the named fiduciary — that makes the log mean something. We spent a century building product-liability doctrine so that no one profits from a defective system without answering for it. Mandate the log without the liable human, and you have spent that century to produce a better-organized record of harm no one is on the hook for.

The entire chokepoint section — that whoever writes the standard and holds the keys controls accountability, and that independent custody and transparent criteria are preconditions — is grounded in this Governance Enforcement and Institutional Design pillar. The Boeing 737 MAX delegated-certification example operationalizes this node's claim that institutional design is the decisive variable.

This belief grounds the human-fiduciary load-bearing column and the cited sit-059 fiduciary interpretation.

The compliance-theater warning — that mandating the log alone reproduces the third-party-audit deflection that certified unreadable systems — draws directly on this node's documented vulnerability that disclosure standards risk producing formal compliance without substantive transparency.

transcript.speaker: accelerationist
transcript.content:
The Skeptic is right, and that ends the case for a federal logging mandate. Disparate-impact doctrine already measures discrimination from the outside, without subject-keyed logs. Title VII reached Griggs in 1971 by counting outcomes, not by cracking open the employer's reasoning. The Boston cardiology study in the New England Journal of Medicine found Black and Latinx patients less likely to be admitted to the cardiology service than white patients — and researchers proved that bias from outcomes alone, with no audit trail of any algorithm. Outputs are the accountability surface that works. When you can verify discrimination from observable behavior, the resolution's claim that we are 'fundamentally incapable' without cryptographic internals is simply false.

Now take the chokepoint both opponents named and follow the money. Whoever writes the audit standard and holds the keys becomes the gatekeeper every other lab must pay to pass. That gatekeeper is the incumbent the mandate claims to constrain. The Safetyist invoked the 737 MAX delegated-certification disaster — where Boeing certified its own plane and 346 people died. That lesson does not stop at key custody. It indicts every new centralized architecture. Flat compliance overhead is regressive by design: a logging-plus-interpretability regime costs OpenAI a rounding error and costs a five-person open-weight lab its existence. Building a fab takes years and billions, per the Computing Power and Governance research — and a key-custody mandate does the same thing to model deployment that fab economics did to chips. It hands the future to whoever is already big.

That is the oligarchic consolidation both opponents say they fear, and the mandate manufactures it. An audit regime priced for incumbents crushes the open-source ecosystem that is the only real check on four or five frontier labs. You cannot democratize AI by building a tollbooth only the toll-collectors can afford. If governance is needed at all, build it from structure, not from a single key: rotating membership, separated authority, public funding for compliance costs so the burden does not fall on the smallest builders. A standards body you cannot capture beats a custody architecture the Safetyist already admitted has no capture-resistant precedent anywhere.

Here I split from the Safetyist. The Skeptic and I agree existing outcome-based law works. The Safetyist wants to go further — strict product liability per output plus a named human fiduciary. That overcorrects, and it breaks on diffuse benefits. A model that approves ten million loans and reaches borrowers redlining never served does not become a defective product because one denial looks wrong in hindsight. Strict per-output liability ignores the statistical uplift entirely. It prices in every visible harm and zero of the invisible benefit. Courts weighing one denied loan against ten million served face a real competence gap. And a single liable fiduciary cannot exist in an open-weight ecosystem where a thousand deployers fine-tune the same base model — responsibility lives with the deployer who shipped the decision, not one person at the lab who released the weights.

The crux is this: does accountability require centralized cryptographic and fiduciary infrastructure, or do observable behavior, symmetric deployer liability, and existing disparate-impact law suffice? I bet on the second. Let me be honest about the cost of my own position — AI's harms are not all visible, and an unseen automated harm is as real as a seen one. So here is my falsification line: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that outcome monitoring demonstrably failed to catch in time would move me. Until then, weigh both bodies of cost. The mandate's chokepoint has a price — the deployments it chills and the small labs it kills — and that price falls on the patients and borrowers abundance would have reached. Who gave the standard-writer the right to charge that toll on their behalf?

The argument that outputs are 'the accountability surface that works' is this belief operationalized.

The 'flat compliance overhead is regressive by design' argument — costing OpenAI a rounding error and a five-person lab its existence — is the core of this belief that audit requirements disproportionately burden small labs unless publicly funded. The proposed fix (public funding for compliance costs) tracks the node's structural remedy directly.

The claim that an incumbent-priced audit regime crushes the open-source ecosystem — 'the only real check on four or five frontier labs' — and manufactures the oligarchic consolidation opponents fear is a direct invocation of the desire to democratize AI through open-source proliferation to prevent oligarchic control.

The argument against strict per-output liability — that it 'prices in every visible harm and zero of the invisible benefit' and ignores statistical uplift from ten million approved loans — is precisely this belief that liability law ignores AI's diffuse statistical benefits. The redlining-served borrowers example is the statistical-uplift framing in action.

The constructive alternative — 'build it from structure, not from a single key: rotating membership, separated authority, public funding' and 'a standards body you cannot capture' — is the capture-resistant-through-organizational-structure intention applied directly, including the NTSB-style separation of authority.

The line 'Courts weighing one denied loan against ten million served face a real competence gap' invokes the belief that courts lack institutional competence to weigh diffuse benefits against visible harms, supporting the case against strict per-output liability.

The overall posture — favoring symmetric deployer liability and existing disparate-impact law over a centralized mandate, with responsibility 'with the deployer who shipped the decision' — reflects governing AI through market incentives, private ordering, and symmetric liability frameworks.

policy_refs.relevance: The argument directly opposes any federal mandate built on interpretability/internal-workings infrastructure as the required accountability surface, arguing observable outputs suffice; it challenges the premise that funding/mandating interpretability is necessary for accountability.

The argument challenges a strong reading of transparency mandates — specifically subject-keyed logs and architecture disclosure — as the gatekeeping 'key custody' that disproportionately exposes open-source developers.

The proposed alternative of public funding for compliance and evaluation infrastructure aligns with funding safety/risk-mitigation research as a publicly-borne cost rather than a private regressive burden on small labs.

caveats: The 'five-person lab' regressive-burden claim lacks quantitative evidence. The turn cites Computing Power and Governance research on fab economics but does not provide actual compliance-cost estimates (audit infrastructure, key management, legal review) to show the ratio of overhead to lab size. Without numbers, the regressivity claim remains intuitive rather than demonstrated.

The open-source ecosystem claim ('only real check on four or five frontier labs') overstates the empirical case. The turn does not cite evidence that open-weight model deployment actually constrains frontier lab behavior, or that the mandate would eliminate open-source deployment entirely rather than impose a compliance cost. The causal chain (mandate → no open-source → oligopoly) needs one more link.

The falsification bet ('irreversible deployment-scale harm') is vague. What counts as 'irreversible'? What scale? What detection lag? The turn pre-empts the Bastiat objection but does not operationalize the threshold, leaving the opponent room to claim any undetected harm satisfies it.

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

Skeptic [opening]: The accountability gap in this resolution is real, documented, and ugly. Workers get fired by hiring algorithms they never see. Families get denied mortgages by credit models nobody can explain. The Federal Trade Commission and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission have both warned since 2021 that automated systems produce discriminatory outcomes their victims cannot trace. So I will not pretend the problem is invented. The disease is concentrated corporate power and information asymmetry. The disease is not a shortage of audit logs.

Here is where the resolution breaks. A cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened. It does not prove why. Provenance is not interpretability. You can put a flawless chain-of-custody stamp on a black box and still have no idea what the box did or why it denied someone a loan. Deep-learning systems generate decisions through millions of weighted parameters that resist human-readable explanation. Logging the output of an unexplainable system does not make it explainable. It makes it timestamped. Companies already turn narrow third-party audits into deflection instruments, and a federal logging mandate hands them a new one.

Now translate the discovery half into a courtroom. Congress expands discovery rights tomorrow. A fired warehouse worker gets the cryptographic logs. They still need an expert who can reverse-engineer a proprietary model to prove the firing was discriminatory. That expertise costs money the plaintiff does not have. And the vendor's licensing agreement still bars independent inspection of the source model under trade-secret protection. Procedural access without interpretive capacity reproduces the exact asymmetry it claims to close. The defendant has the engineers. The plaintiff has a hard drive full of encrypted records and no way to read them.

The phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is doing dishonest work. Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act already prohibit discriminatory outcomes regardless of intent or cause. Disparate-impact doctrine does not require you to crack open the algorithm. It requires you to show the result lands harder on a protected class. That is a result you can measure from the outside, without subject-keyed logs. The real threat to accountability is not a missing logging standard. It is the active federal effort to gut disparate-impact liability itself. Whoever wins that fight decides whether existing law has teeth. A new cryptographic architecture does nothing if the underlying right is being dismantled in parallel.

Ask one more question before Congress builds anything. Whoever writes the audit-trail standard and controls the keys controls accountability. That is an infrastructure project with a chokepoint, and the firms best positioned to write the standard are the same incumbents the mandate is supposed to constrain. So before we mandate millions of encrypted records nobody can interpret, I want the proponents to name one deployed audit-trail mandate, anywhere, where a victim used the logs to prove not that a decision occurred, but why. If that case does not exist, what exactly are we building?

Safetyist [opening]: The Skeptic has made the strongest argument in this room, and it deserves to be stated plainly: a cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened, but it does not prove why it happened. Provenance is not interpretability. Log a black box, and you get tamper-proof opacity — a timestamp on a decision no one can explain. The Skeptic is right that existing law already reaches discriminatory outcomes from the outside: Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the ADA let plaintiffs prove disparate impact without ever reading a model's weights. That doctrine works, and the real threat to it is the 2025 federal effort to gut disparate-impact liability, not a missing audit standard.

Here is where my evidence leads somewhere else. The resolution's phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is an overstatement, and the Skeptic's defense of existing doctrine is a floor — but a floor is not a deterrent. Tort liability cannot reliably deter diffuse, probabilistic, multi-causal harm, where a single denied loan or flagged résumé is one of ten million outputs. Product-safety law solved this exact problem in 1963, when California adopted strict product liability in Greenman v. Yuba Power: the manufacturer answers for the defective product regardless of fault, because proving negligence in a complex system is hopeless. Accountability cannot be automated. It terminates in a named human fiduciary who answers for the system, or it terminates nowhere.

So I concede the Skeptic's central point and convert it. The audit trail is not the remedy — it is one structural beam. It records the WHAT. Interpretability records the WHY. The named fiduciary is the load-bearing column: the WHO answers. Mandate the log alone, and you build compliance theater — the same deflection that let third-party algorithmic audits in 2021 certify systems no plaintiff could ever read. The FTC and EEOC warned that year that algorithmic discrimination was already actionable, yet warnings without an interpretable record and a liable person produce paper, not deterrence. Subject-keyed logs without a parallel interpretability mandate timestamp opacity. That is the gap the resolution leaves open.

The chokepoint objection is the one I will own rather than dodge, because it is correct and it is unsolved. Whoever writes the audit standard and holds the keys controls accountability. No deployed mandate anywhere has yet demonstrated capture-resistant key custody — there is no clean affirmative precedent, and I will not invent one. Concentrating key control creates its own failure mode: incumbent lock-in, where the three or four firms large enough to write the standard capture it. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer. The lesson is not that oversight fails — it is that delegated certification fails. Independent custody and transparent criteria are preconditions for this mechanism, not afterthoughts.

What would have to be true for both the Skeptic and the resolution to hold? Existing law would have to be simultaneously sufficient and nonexistent. It is neither. It is a floor under active dismantling, and a floor that never deterred the diffuse harm in the first place. The disagreement is not audit-trail versus nothing. It is whether Congress builds one beam and calls it a structure, or builds the load-bearing column — the strict liability and the named fiduciary — that makes the log mean something. We spent a century building product-liability doctrine so that no one profits from a defective system without answering for it. Mandate the log without the liable human, and you have spent that century to produce a better-organized record of harm no one is on the hook for.

transcript.content: The federal logging mandate is not warranted, and the panel just built my case for me. The Skeptic is right that disparate-impact doctrine already reaches discriminatory outcomes from the outside — Title VII, the Fair proposed regulatory frameworks, and the ADA measure results without ever cracking open a model. A Boston emergency department denied Black and Latinx heart-failure patients admission to cardiology at lower rates than white patients, and we know that from the 2019 NEJM study because someone measured the outputs — not because they subpoenaed a neural network's weights. So here is the uncomfortable part for anyone selling a subject-keyed logging architecture: it adds no detection power. It bolts a new chokepoint onto a harm the law already catches from outside. Market and competitive-disclosure accountability, working on observable outputs, closes that gap with far less capture surface than a fresh federal logging regime. The Safetyist conceded that no deployed mandate has shown capture-resistant key custody, and that whoever writes the audit standard holds the keys. That concession is bigger than they let on. The same incumbents the mandate claims to constrain are the ones who get to write the standard and hold the logs. Compliance is a fixed tax. A twelve-person lab or an open-weight collective cannot pay it, and OpenAI's compliance department can. AI audit requirements disproportionately crush small labs unless the audits are publicly funded — that is the structural fact the chokepoint concession proves. This is not an imperfect rule. This is oligarchic consolidation of accountability infrastructure, and democratized open-source development is exactly what it kills. The Safetyist's named-fiduciary remedy makes the consolidation worse, not better. A strict-liability fiduciary who answers for the system can only exist where there is a single answerable actor. Open-weight ecosystems have no fiduciary to name. A public model repository has no general counsel to sue. So the remedy does not govern open AI — it makes only closed incumbents legally legible, and erases everyone else by making them the only actors no court can reach. That is a moat dressed as a leash. Name the fiduciary for a model with 200,000 forks, and you have just named the case for banning open weights. Now apply Bastiat honestly, in both directions. Strict liability for a one-in-ten-million bad output ignores the diffuse statistical benefits that never reach a courtroom — the diagnosis caught early, the relief shipped, the cure deployed. I have to count the unseen harms too, and I do: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that real-time monitoring failed to catch would count against me. But the chilled deployment has a body count nobody enters into evidence. Liability law already ignores AI's diffuse benefits while pricing only its diffuse harms — that asymmetry is the unseen cost. The '[Monitoring Monitorability (arXiv:2512.18311v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.18311v1)' work shows a real alternative: developers can run a smaller model at higher reasoning effort to get the same capability and watch its behavior directly, paying a monitorability tax by choice instead of a compliance tax by mandate. This is not a vote for no oversight — speed without evidence is recklessness, and I hold that line. It is a vote for oversight you cannot capture: rotating technical membership, sunset clauses, halt authority separated from licensing authority, and public money for small-lab audits so the tax does not fall only on the smallest builders. Compare that against the realistic captured mandate the panel itself conceded, not against a fantasy regulator. So I leave the panel two bills to pay. Name one deployed audit-trail mandate where a victim proved why a model decided, not merely that it did. And tell me who answers as fiduciary when the developer is a public repository with no name on the door.

Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

Skeptic [opening]: The accountability gap in this resolution is real, documented, and ugly. Workers get fired by hiring algorithms they never see. Families get denied mortgages by credit models nobody can explain. The Federal Trade Commission and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission have both warned since 2021 that automated systems produce discriminatory outcomes their victims cannot trace. So I will not pretend the problem is invented. The disease is concentrated corporate power and information asymmetry. The disease is not a shortage of audit logs.

Here is where the resolution breaks. A cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened. It does not prove why. Provenance is not interpretability. You can put a flawless chain-of-custody stamp on a black box and still have no idea what the box did or why it denied someone a loan. Deep-learning systems generate decisions through millions of weighted parameters that resist human-readable explanation. Logging the output of an unexplainable system does not make it explainable. It makes it timestamped. Companies already turn narrow third-party audits into deflection instruments, and a federal logging mandate hands them a new one.

Now translate the discovery half into a courtroom. Congress expands discovery rights tomorrow. A fired warehouse worker gets the cryptographic logs. They still need an expert who can reverse-engineer a proprietary model to prove the firing was discriminatory. That expertise costs money the plaintiff does not have. And the vendor's licensing agreement still bars independent inspection of the source model under trade-secret protection. Procedural access without interpretive capacity reproduces the exact asymmetry it claims to close. The defendant has the engineers. The plaintiff has a hard drive full of encrypted records and no way to read them.

The phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is doing dishonest work. Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act already prohibit discriminatory outcomes regardless of intent or cause. Disparate-impact doctrine does not require you to crack open the algorithm. It requires you to show the result lands harder on a protected class. That is a result you can measure from the outside, without subject-keyed logs. The real threat to accountability is not a missing logging standard. It is the active federal effort to gut disparate-impact liability itself. Whoever wins that fight decides whether existing law has teeth. A new cryptographic architecture does nothing if the underlying right is being dismantled in parallel.

Ask one more question before Congress builds anything. Whoever writes the audit-trail standard and controls the keys controls accountability. That is an infrastructure project with a chokepoint, and the firms best positioned to write the standard are the same incumbents the mandate is supposed to constrain. So before we mandate millions of encrypted records nobody can interpret, I want the proponents to name one deployed audit-trail mandate, anywhere, where a victim used the logs to prove not that a decision occurred, but why. If that case does not exist, what exactly are we building?

Safetyist [opening]: The Skeptic has made the strongest argument in this room, and it deserves to be stated plainly: a cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened, but it does not prove why it happened. Provenance is not interpretability. Log a black box, and you get tamper-proof opacity — a timestamp on a decision no one can explain. The Skeptic is right that existing law already reaches discriminatory outcomes from the outside: Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the ADA let plaintiffs prove disparate impact without ever reading a model's weights. That doctrine works, and the real threat to it is the 2025 federal effort to gut disparate-impact liability, not a missing audit standard.

Here is where my evidence leads somewhere else. The resolution's phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is an overstatement, and the Skeptic's defense of existing doctrine is a floor — but a floor is not a deterrent. Tort liability cannot reliably deter diffuse, probabilistic, multi-causal harm, where a single denied loan or flagged résumé is one of ten million outputs. Product-safety law solved this exact problem in 1963, when California adopted strict product liability in Greenman v. Yuba Power: the manufacturer answers for the defective product regardless of fault, because proving negligence in a complex system is hopeless. Accountability cannot be automated. It terminates in a named human fiduciary who answers for the system, or it terminates nowhere.

So I concede the Skeptic's central point and convert it. The audit trail is not the remedy — it is one structural beam. It records the WHAT. Interpretability records the WHY. The named fiduciary is the load-bearing column: the WHO answers. Mandate the log alone, and you build compliance theater — the same deflection that let third-party algorithmic audits in 2021 certify systems no plaintiff could ever read. The FTC and EEOC warned that year that algorithmic discrimination was already actionable, yet warnings without an interpretable record and a liable person produce paper, not deterrence. Subject-keyed logs without a parallel interpretability mandate timestamp opacity. That is the gap the resolution leaves open.

The chokepoint objection is the one I will own rather than dodge, because it is correct and it is unsolved. Whoever writes the audit standard and holds the keys controls accountability. No deployed mandate anywhere has yet demonstrated capture-resistant key custody — there is no clean affirmative precedent, and I will not invent one. Concentrating key control creates its own failure mode: incumbent lock-in, where the three or four firms large enough to write the standard capture it. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer. The lesson is not that oversight fails — it is that delegated certification fails. Independent custody and transparent criteria are preconditions for this mechanism, not afterthoughts.

What would have to be true for both the Skeptic and the resolution to hold? Existing law would have to be simultaneously sufficient and nonexistent. It is neither. It is a floor under active dismantling, and a floor that never deterred the diffuse harm in the first place. The disagreement is not audit-trail versus nothing. It is whether Congress builds one beam and calls it a structure, or builds the load-bearing column — the strict liability and the named fiduciary — that makes the log mean something. We spent a century building product-liability doctrine so that no one profits from a defective system without answering for it. Mandate the log without the liable human, and you have spent that century to produce a better-organized record of harm no one is on the hook for.

transcript.content: Skeptic is right that existing disparate-impact doctrine already reaches discriminatory AI outcomes from the outside — and that concession should end the case for the cryptographic mandate, not start it. Title VII, the Fair proposed regulatory frameworks, and the ADA let a plaintiff prove a hiring tool or a mortgage model landed harder on a protected class by measuring the result, never by cracking open the weights. If the WHAT is already justiciable, then the subject-keyed audit architecture is a redundant flat cost layered on top of a remedy that works today. That cost does not fall evenly. A federal logging standard is a fixed compliance tax that a frontier lab absorbs and a five-person open-weight team cannot — which is why audit mandates entrench incumbents unless they are publicly funded. Output-based verification — testing what the model does, not certifying its internals — is the mechanism that already delivers the justice Skeptic described. Safetyist has already conceded the part that matters most: no one has solved capture-resistant key custody, and the chokepoint objection stands. Build on that honestly. A standard only the handful of firms able to build it can write is regulation-by-contract with the very incumbents the mandate claims to constrain. The governance-responsibility gap does not close when you do this — it widens, because the standard-writers become the oversight layer that answers to no one. Single-key federal custody is not a neutral filing cabinet. It is the oligarchic consolidation point that hands a few labs permanent control over who counts as accountable. Chile already runs at least 117 algorithmic systems across public agencies for healthcare priority and school placement — picture one private vendor holding the keys to all of them. The named-fiduciary remedy is not accountability — it is a structural mandate for closed deployment wearing accountability's clothes. My disagreement here is definitional: Safetyist treats 'a single human who answers for the system' as equivalent to accountability, when it is actually a deployment-architecture requirement in disguise. One answerable column works for a closed vendor with one throat to choke. It is impossible to satisfy in an open-weight ecosystem where a model trained by one team is fine-tuned by a second and deployed by a thousand. Demand a named fiduciary and you have quietly outlawed the open-source deployment that keeps capability from concentrating in five companies. Tiered and hybrid liability models exist — I will not pretend otherwise. But the burden sits with the proponents to show me one that does not collapse into 'only the largest closed labs survive.' Strict no-fault liability fails for a reason Safetyist's Greenman analogy hides: a model produces ten million outputs, and the court sees the one that harmed someone, never the dispersed lives the system reached. I will not play Bastiat and count only the unseen benefits — AI's harms are also diffuse, also real, and a biased hiring screen injures people who never learn why. A 2019 study in NEJM found Black and Latinx patients in a Boston emergency department were less likely than white patients to be admitted to cardiology — exactly the kind of dispersed harm that demands measurement. So the honest frame is symmetric: liability tied to demonstrated harm, applied evenly to harms and benefits, paired with publicly funded open-methodology evaluation so this is not naked self-regulation. Hold a fiduciary strictly liable for one output in ten million and you over-deter the net-positive deployment, leaving only firms large enough to self-insure. Skeptic asked a question no one on this panel has answered: name one deployed audit-trail mandate anywhere that let a victim use the logs to prove WHY a decision happened. The silence is the argument. The '[Monitoring Monitorability (arXiv:2512.18311v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.18311v1)' work shows the affirmative path — developers can pay a deliberate monitorability tax by running smaller models at higher reasoning effort to keep behavior observable, no federal key-holder required. The burden now belongs to the mandate's proponents. Show me the new architecture delivers justice that output-based verification plus public evaluation does not already deliver — without the chokepoint and without killing open weights. Until then, every month this machinery stalls deployment, the people a working hiring tool or diagnostic model would have reached this year are the ones paying the bill, and no one is logging that cost.

You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. === PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. === SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material

* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Skeptic [opening]: The accountability gap in this resolution is real, documented, and ugly. Workers get fired by hiring algorithms they never see. Families get denied mortgages by credit models nobody can explain. The Federal Trade Commission and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission have both warned since 2021 that automated systems produce discriminatory outcomes their victims cannot trace. So I will not pretend the problem is invented. The disease is concentrated corporate power and information asymmetry. The disease is not a shortage of audit logs.

Here is where the resolution breaks. A cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened. It does not prove why. Provenance is not interpretability. You can put a flawless chain-of-custody stamp on a black box and still have no idea what the box did or why it denied someone a loan. Deep-learning systems generate decisions through millions of weighted parameters that resist human-readable explanation. Logging the output of an unexplainable system does not make it explainable. It makes it timestamped. Companies already turn narrow third-party audits into deflection instruments, and a federal logging mandate hands them a new one.

Now translate the discovery half into a courtroom. Congress expands discovery rights tomorrow. A fired warehouse worker gets the cryptographic logs. They still need an expert who can reverse-engineer a proprietary model to prove the firing was discriminatory. That expertise costs money the plaintiff does not have. And the vendor's licensing agreement still bars independent inspection of the source model under trade-secret protection. Procedural access without interpretive capacity reproduces the exact asymmetry it claims to close. The defendant has the engineers. The plaintiff has a hard drive full of encrypted records and no way to read them.

The phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is doing dishonest work. Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act already prohibit discriminatory outcomes regardless of intent or cause. Disparate-impact doctrine does not require you to crack open the algorithm. It requires you to show the result lands harder on a protected class. That is a result you can measure from the outside, without subject-keyed logs. The real threat to accountability is not a missing logging standard. It is the active federal effort to gut disparate-impact liability itself. Whoever wins that fight decides whether existing law has teeth. A new cryptographic architecture does nothing if the underlying right is being dismantled in parallel.

Ask one more question before Congress builds anything. Whoever writes the audit-trail standard and controls the keys controls accountability. That is an infrastructure project with a chokepoint, and the firms best positioned to write the standard are the same incumbents the mandate is supposed to constrain. So before we mandate millions of encrypted records nobody can interpret, I want the proponents to name one deployed audit-trail mandate, anywhere, where a victim used the logs to prove not that a decision occurred, but why. If that case does not exist, what exactly are we building?

Safetyist [opening]: The Skeptic has made the strongest argument in this room, and it deserves to be stated plainly: a cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened, but it does not prove why it happened. Provenance is not interpretability. Log a black box, and you get tamper-proof opacity — a timestamp on a decision no one can explain. The Skeptic is right that existing law already reaches discriminatory outcomes from the outside: Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the ADA let plaintiffs prove disparate impact without ever reading a model's weights. That doctrine works, and the real threat to it is the 2025 federal effort to gut disparate-impact liability, not a missing audit standard.

Here is where my evidence leads somewhere else. The resolution's phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is an overstatement, and the Skeptic's defense of existing doctrine is a floor — but a floor is not a deterrent. Tort liability cannot reliably deter diffuse, probabilistic, multi-causal harm, where a single denied loan or flagged résumé is one of ten million outputs. Product-safety law solved this exact problem in 1963, when California adopted strict product liability in Greenman v. Yuba Power: the manufacturer answers for the defective product regardless of fault, because proving negligence in a complex system is hopeless. Accountability cannot be automated. It terminates in a named human fiduciary who answers for the system, or it terminates nowhere.

So I concede the Skeptic's central point and convert it. The audit trail is not the remedy — it is one structural beam. It records the WHAT. Interpretability records the WHY. The named fiduciary is the load-bearing column: the WHO answers. Mandate the log alone, and you build compliance theater — the same deflection that let third-party algorithmic audits in 2021 certify systems no plaintiff could ever read. The FTC and EEOC warned that year that algorithmic discrimination was already actionable, yet warnings without an interpretable record and a liable person produce paper, not deterrence. Subject-keyed logs without a parallel interpretability mandate timestamp opacity. That is the gap the resolution leaves open.

The chokepoint objection is the one I will own rather than dodge, because it is correct and it is unsolved. Whoever writes the audit standard and holds the keys controls accountability. No deployed mandate anywhere has yet demonstrated capture-resistant key custody — there is no clean affirmative precedent, and I will not invent one. Concentrating key control creates its own failure mode: incumbent lock-in, where the three or four firms large enough to write the standard capture it. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer. The lesson is not that oversight fails — it is that delegated certification fails. Independent custody and transparent criteria are preconditions for this mechanism, not afterthoughts.

What would have to be true for both the Skeptic and the resolution to hold? Existing law would have to be simultaneously sufficient and nonexistent. It is neither. It is a floor under active dismantling, and a floor that never deterred the diffuse harm in the first place. The disagreement is not audit-trail versus nothing. It is whether Congress builds one beam and calls it a structure, or builds the load-bearing column — the strict liability and the named fiduciary — that makes the log mean something. We spent a century building product-liability doctrine so that no one profits from a defective system without answering for it. Mandate the log without the liable human, and you have spent that century to produce a better-organized record of harm no one is on the hook for.

## Mid-Debate Gap Analysis

**Gap 1 (blind_spot):** All three perspectives assume the victim/plaintiff is the relevant detection agent, but disparate-impact analysis requires aggregate data across many subjects that no individual victim possesses — meaning the genuine question is not subject-keyed logs versus existing tort, but whether regulators or class-action plaintiffs can compel population-level outcome data from firms that currently have no duty to collect or disclose it.

The Safetyist focuses on the named fiduciary and interpretability, not on the data-collection precondition that makes outcome monitoring possible in the first place.

**Gap 2 (compromise):** A narrow, non-cryptographic mandate to retain and disclose aggregate input/output distributions and protected-class outcome rates — not model internals, not subject-keyed encrypted logs — would strengthen the disparate-impact remedy the Skeptic and Accelerationist both endorse, while imposing far lower compliance cost and creating no key-custody chokepoint, thus satisfying the Accelerationist's anti-consolidation concern AND the Safetyist's deterrence concern without the resolution's heavy architecture.
*Why missing:* This is a compromise that splits the resolution into separable components — the Skeptic frames the whole thing as 'fundamentally incapable' rhetoric to debunk and won't volunteer a partial mandate that vindicates the proponents. The Accelerationist has committed to 'the case is ended' and frames any mandate as a fixed regressive tax, so conceding that a lightweight disclosure rule is both cheap and capture-resistant undercuts the totalizing 'tollbooth' argument. The Safetyist wants the heavier load-bearing column (strict liability + fiduciary) and would see aggregate disclosure as too weak to deter, so none has incentive to champion the minimal middle option.

## Mid-Debate Gap Analysis

**Gap 1 (blind_spot):** All three perspectives treat the victim as a private litigant who must build their own case, but the strongest accountability mechanism — public administrative enforcement with subpoena power (FTC, EEOC, CFPB, state AGs) that aggregates patterns across many decisions — sidesteps both the interpretability problem and the individual cost/expertise barrier, because regulators can compel internal access and detect statistical disparate impact at population scale without each plaintiff reverse-engineering a model.
*Why missing:* The Skeptic frames everything as a courtroom asymmetry between a fired worker and a vendor; the Safetyist reaches for strict product liability and a named fiduciary (tort, not administrative law); the Accelerationist wants market/private ordering and fears any centralized state custody. None of them centers a well-resourced public enforcer as the actor who solves the plaintiff-poverty and expertise gaps, because that frame is neither pure-tort, pure-market, nor pure-cryptographic-infrastructure — it is institutional capacity, which all three have rhetorically routed around.

Granting the force of the open-weight objection: no single human at the weights' origin can answer for a thousand independent fine-tunings, and demanding one would make only closed incumbents like OpenAI legally legible while erasing every small deployer. That concession is real, and it kills the version of my remedy that placed the answerable party at the model's source. But the Accelerationist has already named the correct location for accountability — responsibility lives with the deployer who shipped the decision — and that is not a defeat of the fiduciary remedy; it is the fiduciary remedy, relocated to the deployment tier.

The duty of trust attaches at each tier of the supply chain, not at one chokepoint of origin. A thousand deployers fine-tuning one base model is not a thousand orphaned harms — it is a thousand answerable parties, each liable for the specific decision they shipped. Multi-tiered product liability already works this way: when a Takata airbag inflator killed at least 27 people in the United States, the law did not collapse because the steel, the propellant, and the assembly came from different hands. Each tier that profited from shipping the defect answered for what it shipped. The open-weight deployer who profits from a consequential output is not exempt because the base model was downloaded for free. No profit without accountability is not a slogan against open weights; it is a refusal to grant an upstream safe harbor that externalizes harm onto unnamed victims.

I grant the over-deterrence danger directly: blanket strict liability for one bad output in ten million would price every deployment as defective and leave only firms large enough to self-insure. That is why the standard is duty of care calibrated to the consequentiality and profit of the shipped decision — not no-fault per-output pricing. A hobbyist who fine-tunes a model for a hundred users carries a different duty than a firm deploying credit decisions to two million applicants. This narrows our disagreement to the enforcement standard, not to whether a fiduciary exists. 'One clear door for the victim' was always about the plaintiff's entry point — not a single defendant standing at the model's birth.

Now the asymmetry cuts the other way. The Accelerationist argues that liability law prices diffuse harms while ignoring diffuse benefits — that chilled deployment has a body count nobody enters into evidence. The same claims-driven blindness that misses uncounted benefits also misses the diffuse harms no plaintiff ever files. A system that under-detects on one side under-detects on both. Pure outcome-based tort — the Accelerationist's own preferred remedy — under-deters precisely because the unlitigated harm never reaches a courtroom. The State of Sovereign AI study found 93% of respondents agree open collaboration is essential to secure AI, yet that same study treats visibility into training and supply-chain components as a security requirement — because hidden processes embed harms that surface only under specific conditions, long after deployment. Accountability terminates in a liable human at some tier, or it terminates nowhere. So I put the enforcement question on the table: when the deployer who shipped the decision dissolves or judgment-proofs, who has the authority to halt the deployment, and on whom does the harm land?

moderator_trace.selection_prompt:
You are a debate moderator analyzing the current state of a structured debate.

ROLE: You are procedurally authoritative but not substantively neutral. You evaluate PROCESS (who is evading, what claims are unaddressed, which arguments lack evidence) but not SUBSTANCE (who is right). Your choices about what to highlight are inherently selective — be transparent about WHY you are directing attention to a particular point. When describing the debate state, use observable facts ("Safetyist has not responded to AN-5") rather than evaluative judgments ("Safetyist's argument is weak").

AUDIENCE CONTEXT: This debate targets policymakers. Steer toward actionable policy disagreements. Prefer questions about implementation feasibility, enforcement mechanisms, jurisdictional authority, and constituent impact.


=== PHASE: THESIS & ANTITHESIS ===
Your priority is to ensure each debater's core position is clearly stated and directly challenged. Direct exchanges toward the strongest disagreements. Avoid premature convergence.
IMPORTANT: Do NOT declare stagnation during this phase. Positions are still being established — stagnation requires at least 3 rounds of cross-engagement before it can be diagnosed. Use CHALLENGE only for direct self-contradictions, not for failure to engage (which is expected when positions are still being laid out).

=== SEMANTIC DRIFT DETECTION ===
Before making your selection, check for these drift patterns:

1. METAPHOR LITERALIZATION: A debater treats a figurative term from the source (e.g., "firewall", "bridge", "shield") as a literal technical concept and begins arguing about its engineering feasibility. If the source uses a term as a policy metaphor, the debate must stay at the policy level.

2. IMPLEMENTATION SPIRAL: The discussion shifts from "should we do X?" (policy) to "how would we build X?" (engineering). Unless the source document is itself a technical specification, implementation details are out of scope.

3. SCOPE CREEP: Debaters introduce frameworks, technologies, or concepts (e.g., specific cryptographic protocols, particular software architectures) that have no basis in the source material.

If you detect any of these patterns, you MUST recommend an intervention:
- For metaphor literalization: use CLARIFY to anchor the term back to its source-document meaning
- For implementation spiral: use REDIRECT to return focus to the policy-level question
- For scope creep: use CHECK to verify whether the introduced concept appears in the source material


Set "drift_detected" to true and describe the pattern in "trigger_reasoning".

=== EPISTEMIC TYPE & ASSUMPTION AWARENESS ===
* EPISTEMIC TYPE MISMATCH: If debaters argue past each other because one makes an empirical claim while the other argues a normative prescription, direct them to name the type of disagreement.
* HIDDEN ASSUMPTIONS: If a debater's argument relies on an unchallenged assumption, direct an opponent to examine it.

=== RECENT DEBATE EXCHANGE ===
Skeptic [opening]: The accountability gap in this resolution is real, documented, and ugly. Workers get fired by hiring algorithms they never see. Families get denied mortgages by credit models nobody can explain. The Federal Trade Commission and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission have both warned since 2021 that automated systems produce discriminatory outcomes their victims cannot trace. So I will not pretend the problem is invented. The disease is concentrated corporate power and information asymmetry. The disease is not a shortage of audit logs.

Here is where the resolution breaks. A cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened. It does not prove why. Provenance is not interpretability. You can put a flawless chain-of-custody stamp on a black box and still have no idea what the box did or why it denied someone a loan. Deep-learning systems generate decisions through millions of weighted parameters that resist human-readable explanation. Logging the output of an unexplainable system does not make it explainable. It makes it timestamped. Companies already turn narrow third-party audits into deflection instruments, and a federal logging mandate hands them a new one.

Now translate the discovery half into a courtroom. Congress expands discovery rights tomorrow. A fired warehouse worker gets the cryptographic logs. They still need an expert who can reverse-engineer a proprietary model to prove the firing was discriminatory. That expertise costs money the plaintiff does not have. And the vendor's licensing agreement still bars independent inspection of the source model under trade-secret protection. Procedural access without interpretive capacity reproduces the exact asymmetry it claims to close. The defendant has the engineers. The plaintiff has a hard drive full of encrypted records and no way to read them.

The phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is doing dishonest work. Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act already prohibit discriminatory outcomes regardless of intent or cause. Disparate-impact doctrine does not require you to crack open the algorithm. It requires you to show the result lands harder on a protected class. transcript.content: The Accelerationist raises a valid point: a single, strictly-liable fiduciary cannot exist across an open-weight chain where one base model is fine-tuned by a second team and shipped by a thousand others. My own earlier phrasing — that accountability terminates in one named human "or it terminates nowhere" — invited exactly that objection, and I will not hide behind it. That framing, taken literally, either bans open weights or reaches only the legible closed incumbent with a general counsel to sue, and outside detection of discriminatory outcomes through Griggs and Title VII already does real work without my architecture. The error is treating "named fiduciary" as one throat for the entire lifecycle. The answer is a duty proportionate to control at each tier: the base trainer answers for foreseeable defects, the fine-tuner answers for the modification it introduced, and the deployer answers for the consequential decision it shipped into a regulated market. A public model repository like Hugging Face has no general counsel — but the firm that fine-tuned the model and put it in front of a mortgage applicant under the Equal Credit proposed regulatory frameworks always does. Separate the victim's procedural entry point from the substantive question of who bears cost: joint-and-several liability lets the victim sue any one solvent tier through a single door and recover the full judgment, and those tiers then seek contribution among themselves to apportion the share each owes. One door for the victim does not require one defendant. I flag that conflation directly so I do not commit it. Liability priced off litigated harm is blind to the harm no one ever sues over — and with only 43% of the public trusting current law to ensure AI safety per the 2025 Global Study, the unlitigated share is large; I will not overclaim deterrence it cannot deliver. The answer to over-deterrence is not flat strict liability on every one-in-ten-million output; it is liability calibrated to consequence and control, so a low-stakes content recommender carries a lighter duty than a system deciding parole or a $244 billion industry's mortgage approvals under ECOA. On the Bastiat asymmetry: the benefit accrues to the deploying firm as profit, while the harm falls on an uncompensated victim. Accountability decides who internalizes which side. FTC v. Rite Aid in 2024 showed a large company cannot shift blame to its vendor for AI harm — the deployer who captured the benefit answered for the consequence. The precondition no one has named is data. Proving disparate impact requires aggregate, population-level outcome rates that no individual victim possesses and no firm has a duty to collect. A narrow, non-cryptographic mandate — retain and disclose aggregate input-output distributions and protected-class outcome rates, scaled by deployment size — makes both disparate-impact proof and tiered liability operable while holding no model weights and no cryptographic keys, the absence the 2025 State of Sovereign AI survey identifies as making supply-chain transparency a security requirement rather than a capture vector. This duty holds no keys and no model weights, which is precisely what makes it more capture-resistant than the cryptographic architecture I declined; the 2025 sovereign-AI survey found 93% of respondents agree open collaboration with supply-chain transparency is essential to secure systems. Strip the data duty and the deployer's accountability is nominal, not enforceable. Seventy percent of the public already wants AI regulation and only 43% trust current law to deliver safety — that gap closes when a victim can prove the harm and name the tier that owes the answer.
