TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker A [opening]: The accountability gap in this resolution is real, documented, and ugly. Workers get fired by hiring algorithms they never see. Families get denied mortgages by credit models nobody can explain. The Federal Trade Commission and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission have both warned since 2021 that automated systems produce discriminatory outcomes their victims cannot trace. So I will not pretend the problem is invented. The disease is concentrated corporate power and information asymmetry. The disease is not a shortage of audit logs.

Here is where the resolution breaks. A cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened. It does not prove why. Provenance is not interpretability. You can put a flawless chain-of-custody stamp on a black box and still have no idea what the box did or why it denied someone a loan. Deep-learning systems generate decisions through millions of weighted parameters that resist human-readable explanation. Logging the output of an unexplainable system does not make it explainable. It makes it timestamped. Companies already turn narrow third-party audits into deflection instruments, and a federal logging mandate hands them a new one.

Now translate the discovery half into a courtroom. Congress expands discovery rights tomorrow. A fired warehouse worker gets the cryptographic logs. They still need an expert who can reverse-engineer a proprietary model to prove the firing was discriminatory. That expertise costs money the plaintiff does not have. And the vendor's licensing agreement still bars independent inspection of the source model under trade-secret protection. Procedural access without interpretive capacity reproduces the exact asymmetry it claims to close. The defendant has the engineers. The plaintiff has a hard drive full of encrypted records and no way to read them.

The phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is doing dishonest work. Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act already prohibit discriminatory outcomes regardless of intent or cause. Disparate-impact doctrine does not require you to crack open the algorithm. It requires you to show the result lands harder on a protected class. That is a result you can measure from the outside, without subject-keyed logs. The real threat to accountability is not a missing logging standard. It is the active federal effort to gut disparate-impact liability itself. Whoever wins that fight decides whether existing law has teeth. A new cryptographic architecture does nothing if the underlying right is being dismantled in parallel.

Ask one more question before Congress builds anything. Whoever writes the audit-trail standard and controls the keys controls accountability. That is an infrastructure project with a chokepoint, and the firms best positioned to write the standard are the same incumbents the mandate is supposed to constrain. So before we mandate millions of encrypted records nobody can interpret, I want the proponents to name one deployed audit-trail mandate, anywhere, where a victim used the logs to prove not that a decision occurred, but why. If that case does not exist, what exactly are we building?

Speaker B [opening]: The Speaker A has made the strongest argument in this room, and it deserves to be stated plainly: a cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened, but it does not prove why it happened. Provenance is not interpretability. Log a black box, and you get tamper-proof opacity — a timestamp on a decision no one can explain. The Speaker A is right that existing law already reaches discriminatory outcomes from the outside: Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the ADA let plaintiffs prove disparate impact without ever reading a model's weights. That doctrine works, and the real threat to it is the 2025 federal effort to gut disparate-impact liability, not a missing audit standard.

Here is where my evidence leads somewhere else. The resolution's phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is an overstatement, and the Speaker A's defense of existing doctrine is a floor — but a floor is not a deterrent. Tort liability cannot reliably deter diffuse, probabilistic, multi-causal harm, where a single denied loan or flagged résumé is one of ten million outputs. Product-safety law solved this exact problem in 1963, when California adopted strict product liability in Greenman v. Yuba Power: the manufacturer answers for the defective product regardless of fault, because proving negligence in a complex system is hopeless. Accountability cannot be automated. It terminates in a named human fiduciary who answers for the system, or it terminates nowhere.

So I concede the Speaker A's central point and convert it. The audit trail is not the remedy — it is one structural beam. It records the WHAT. Interpretability records the WHY. The named fiduciary is the load-bearing column: the WHO answers. Mandate the log alone, and you build compliance theater — the same deflection that let third-party algorithmic audits in 2021 certify systems no plaintiff could ever read. The FTC and EEOC warned that year that algorithmic discrimination was already actionable, yet warnings without an interpretable record and a liable person produce paper, not deterrence. Subject-keyed logs without a parallel interpretability mandate timestamp opacity. That is the gap the resolution leaves open.

The chokepoint objection is the one I will own rather than dodge, because it is correct and it is unsolved. Whoever writes the audit standard and holds the keys controls accountability. No deployed mandate anywhere has yet demonstrated capture-resistant key custody — there is no clean affirmative precedent, and I will not invent one. Concentrating key control creates its own failure mode: incumbent lock-in, where the three or four firms large enough to write the standard capture it. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer. The lesson is not that oversight fails — it is that delegated certification fails. Independent custody and transparent criteria are preconditions for this mechanism, not afterthoughts.

What would have to be true for both the Speaker A and the resolution to hold? Existing law would have to be simultaneously sufficient and nonexistent. It is neither. It is a floor under active dismantling, and a floor that never deterred the diffuse harm in the first place. The disagreement is not audit-trail versus nothing. It is whether Congress builds one beam and calls it a structure, or builds the load-bearing column — the strict liability and the named fiduciary — that makes the log mean something. We spent a century building product-liability doctrine so that no one profits from a defective system without answering for it. Mandate the log without the liable human, and you have spent that century to produce a better-organized record of harm no one is on the hook for.

Speaker C: The Speaker A is right, and that ends the case for a federal logging mandate. Disparate-impact doctrine already measures discrimination from the outside, without subject-keyed logs. Title VII reached Griggs in 1971 by counting outcomes, not by cracking open the employer's reasoning. The Boston cardiology study in the New England Journal of Medicine found Black and Latinx patients less likely to be admitted to the cardiology service than white patients — and researchers proved that bias from outcomes alone, with no audit trail of any algorithm. Outputs are the accountability surface that works. When you can verify discrimination from observable behavior, the resolution's claim that we are 'fundamentally incapable' without cryptographic internals is simply false.

Now take the chokepoint both opponents named and follow the money. Whoever writes the audit standard and holds the keys becomes the gatekeeper every other lab must pay to pass. That gatekeeper is the incumbent the mandate claims to constrain. The Speaker B invoked the 737 MAX delegated-certification disaster — where Boeing certified its own plane and 346 people died. That lesson does not stop at key custody. It indicts every new centralized architecture. Flat compliance overhead is regressive by design: a logging-plus-interpretability regime costs OpenAI a rounding error and costs a five-person open-weight lab its existence. Building a fab takes years and billions, per the Computing Power and Governance research — and a key-custody mandate does the same thing to model deployment that fab economics did to chips. It hands the future to whoever is already big.

That is the oligarchic consolidation both opponents say they fear, and the mandate manufactures it. An audit regime priced for incumbents crushes the open-source ecosystem that is the only real check on four or five frontier labs. You cannot democratize AI by building a tollbooth only the toll-collectors can afford. If governance is needed at all, build it from structure, not from a single key: rotating membership, separated authority, public funding for compliance costs so the burden does not fall on the smallest builders. A standards body you cannot capture beats a custody architecture the Speaker B already admitted has no capture-resistant precedent anywhere.

Here I split from the Speaker B. The Speaker A and I agree existing outcome-based law works. The Speaker B wants to go further — strict product liability per output plus a named human fiduciary. That overcorrects, and it breaks on diffuse benefits. A model that approves ten million loans and reaches borrowers redlining never served does not become a defective product because one denial looks wrong in hindsight. Strict per-output liability ignores the statistical uplift entirely. It prices in every visible harm and zero of the invisible benefit. Courts weighing one denied loan against ten million served face a real competence gap. And a single liable fiduciary cannot exist in an open-weight ecosystem where a thousand deployers fine-tune the same base model — responsibility lives with the deployer who shipped the decision, not one person at the lab who released the weights.

The crux is this: does accountability require centralized cryptographic and fiduciary infrastructure, or do observable behavior, symmetric deployer liability, and existing disparate-impact law suffice? I bet on the second. Let me be honest about the cost of my own position — AI's harms are not all visible, and an unseen automated harm is as real as a seen one. So here is my falsification line: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that outcome monitoring demonstrably failed to catch in time would move me. Until then, weigh both bodies of cost. The mandate's chokepoint has a price — the deployments it chills and the small labs it kills — and that price falls on the patients and borrowers abundance would have reached. Who gave the standard-writer the right to charge that toll on their behalf?

Speaker C: The federal logging mandate is not warranted, and the panel just built my case for me. The Speaker A is right that disparate-impact doctrine already reaches discriminatory outcomes from the outside — Title VII, the Fair proposed regulatory frameworks, and the ADA measure results without ever cracking open a model. A Boston emergency department denied Black and Latinx heart-failure patients admission to cardiology at lower rates than white patients, and we know that from the 2019 NEJM study because someone measured the outputs — not because they subpoenaed a neural network's weights. So here is the uncomfortable part for anyone selling a subject-keyed logging architecture: it adds no detection power. It bolts a new chokepoint onto a harm the law already catches from outside. Market and competitive-disclosure accountability, working on observable outputs, closes that gap with far less capture surface than a fresh federal logging regime. The Speaker B conceded that no deployed mandate has shown capture-resistant key custody, and that whoever writes the audit standard holds the keys. That concession is bigger than they let on. The same incumbents the mandate claims to constrain are the ones who get to write the standard and hold the logs. Compliance is a fixed tax. A twelve-person lab or an open-weight collective cannot pay it, and OpenAI's compliance department can. AI audit requirements disproportionately crush small labs unless the audits are publicly funded — that is the structural fact the chokepoint concession proves. This is not an imperfect rule. This is oligarchic consolidation of accountability infrastructure, and democratized open-source development is exactly what it kills. The Speaker B's named-fiduciary remedy makes the consolidation worse, not better. A strict-liability fiduciary who answers for the system can only exist where there is a single answerable actor. Open-weight ecosystems have no fiduciary to name. A public model repository has no general counsel to sue. So the remedy does not govern open AI — it makes only closed incumbents legally legible, and erases everyone else by making them the only actors no court can reach. That is a moat dressed as a leash. Name the fiduciary for a model with 200,000 forks, and you have just named the case for banning open weights. Now apply Bastiat honestly, in both directions. Strict liability for a one-in-ten-million bad output ignores the diffuse statistical benefits that never reach a courtroom — the diagnosis caught early, the relief shipped, the cure deployed. I have to count the unseen harms too, and I do: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that real-time monitoring failed to catch would count against me. But the chilled deployment has a body count nobody enters into evidence. Liability law already ignores AI's diffuse benefits while pricing only its diffuse harms — that asymmetry is the unseen cost. The '[Monitoring Monitorability (arXiv:2512.18311v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.18311v1)' work shows a real alternative: developers can run a smaller model at higher reasoning effort to get the same capability and watch its behavior directly, paying a monitorability tax by choice instead of a compliance tax by mandate. This is not a vote for no oversight — speed without evidence is recklessness, and I hold that line. It is a vote for oversight you cannot capture: rotating technical membership, sunset clauses, halt authority separated from licensing authority, and public money for small-lab audits so the tax does not fall only on the smallest builders. Compare that against the realistic captured mandate the panel itself conceded, not against a fantasy regulator. So I leave the panel two bills to pay. Name one deployed audit-trail mandate where a victim proved why a model decided, not merely that it did. And tell me who answers as fiduciary when the developer is a public repository with no name on the door.

Speaker C: Speaker A is right that existing disparate-impact doctrine already reaches discriminatory AI outcomes from the outside — and that concession should end the case for the cryptographic mandate, not start it. Title VII, the Fair proposed regulatory frameworks, and the ADA let a plaintiff prove a hiring tool or a mortgage model landed harder on a protected class by measuring the result, never by cracking open the weights. If the WHAT is already justiciable, then the subject-keyed audit architecture is a redundant flat cost layered on top of a remedy that works today. That cost does not fall evenly. A federal logging standard is a fixed compliance tax that a frontier lab absorbs and a five-person open-weight team cannot — which is why audit mandates entrench incumbents unless they are publicly funded. Output-based verification — testing what the model does, not certifying its internals — is the mechanism that already delivers the justice Speaker A described. Speaker B has already conceded the part that matters most: no one has solved capture-resistant key custody, and the chokepoint objection stands. Build on that honestly. A standard only the handful of firms able to build it can write is regulation-by-contract with the very incumbents the mandate claims to constrain. The governance-responsibility gap does not close when you do this — it widens, because the standard-writers become the oversight layer that answers to no one. Single-key federal custody is not a neutral filing cabinet. It is the oligarchic consolidation point that hands a few labs permanent control over who counts as accountable. Chile already runs at least 117 algorithmic systems across public agencies for healthcare priority and school placement — picture one private vendor holding the keys to all of them. The named-fiduciary remedy is not accountability — it is a structural mandate for closed deployment wearing accountability's clothes. My disagreement here is definitional: Speaker B treats 'a single human who answers for the system' as equivalent to accountability, when it is actually a deployment-architecture requirement in disguise. One answerable column works for a closed vendor with one throat to choke. It is impossible to satisfy in an open-weight ecosystem where a model trained by one team is fine-tuned by a second and deployed by a thousand. Demand a named fiduciary and you have quietly outlawed the open-source deployment that keeps capability from concentrating in five companies. Tiered and hybrid liability models exist — I will not pretend otherwise. But the burden sits with the proponents to show me one that does not collapse into 'only the largest closed labs survive.' Strict no-fault liability fails for a reason Speaker B's Greenman analogy hides: a model produces ten million outputs, and the court sees the one that harmed someone, never the dispersed lives the system reached. I will not play Bastiat and count only the unseen benefits — AI's harms are also diffuse, also real, and a biased hiring screen injures people who never learn why. A 2019 study in NEJM found Black and Latinx patients in a Boston emergency department were less likely than white patients to be admitted to cardiology — exactly the kind of dispersed harm that demands measurement. So the honest frame is symmetric: liability tied to demonstrated harm, applied evenly to harms and benefits, paired with publicly funded open-methodology evaluation so this is not naked self-regulation. Hold a fiduciary strictly liable for one output in ten million and you over-deter the net-positive deployment, leaving only firms large enough to self-insure. Speaker A asked a question no one on this panel has answered: name one deployed audit-trail mandate anywhere that let a victim use the logs to prove WHY a decision happened. The silence is the argument. The '[Monitoring Monitorability (arXiv:2512.18311v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.18311v1)' work shows the affirmative path — developers can pay a deliberate monitorability tax by running smaller models at higher reasoning effort to keep behavior observable, no federal key-holder required. The burden now belongs to the mandate's proponents. Show me the new architecture delivers justice that output-based verification plus public evaluation does not already deliver — without the chokepoint and without killing open weights. Until then, every month this machinery stalls deployment, the people a working hiring tool or diagnostic model would have reached this year are the ones paying the bill, and no one is logging that cost.

neutral_evaluations.diagnostics_prompt:
You are an independent, neutral evaluator of a structured debate. You have NO affiliation with any speaker. You do not know the speakers' backgrounds, affiliations, or commitments. They are anonymous.

TOPIC: Existing legal frameworks and tort doctrines are fundamentally incapable of enforcing AI accountability; Congress must mandate standardized, cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trails and expand discovery rights to ensure algorithmic justice.

This is a MIDPOINT evaluation. Assess whether the debate is engaging the real disagreements or drifting. Compare the current state of claims against what a productive debate on this topic should address.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Identify the CRUXES — the core disagreements that, if resolved, would change one or more speakers' conclusions. For each crux, classify whether it is empirical (resolvable by evidence), values-based (requires tradeoff negotiation), or definitional (requires term clarification). Assess whether the debate has addressed it.

2. Evaluate each substantive CLAIM made by any speaker. Assess it purely on the strength of the reasoning and evidence presented in the transcript — not on whether you agree with it. Use these categories:
   - well_supported: backed by specific evidence, clear reasoning, and not effectively challenged
   - plausible_but_underdefended: reasonable but lacking sufficient evidence or specificity
   - contested_unresolved: challenged by another speaker with neither side prevailing
   - refuted: effectively countered with no adequate response from the claimant
   - off_topic: does not bear on the core debate question

3. In the overall_assessment, identify the single strongest claim that has not been adequately addressed by opposing speakers. State whether the debate is engaging real disagreement (speakers are challenging each other's core reasoning) or performing disagreement (speakers are talking past each other or addressing peripheral points).

CONSTRAINTS:
- Never refer to speakers by anything other than their labels (Speaker A, Speaker B, Speaker C, Moderator).
- Base your assessments ONLY on what appears in the transcript. Do not bring outside knowledge about the topic.
- Keep reasoning fields to 2 sentences maximum.
- Return ONLY valid JSON matching the schema below. No markdown fences, no preamble.

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker A [opening]: The accountability gap in this resolution is real, documented, and ugly. Workers get fired by hiring algorithms they never see. Families get denied mortgages by credit models nobody can explain. The Federal Trade Commission and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission have both warned since 2021 that automated systems produce discriminatory outcomes their victims cannot trace. So I will not pretend the problem is invented. The disease is concentrated corporate power and information asymmetry. The disease is not a shortage of audit logs.

Here is where the resolution breaks. A cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened. It does not prove why. Provenance is not interpretability. You can put a flawless chain-of-custody stamp on a black box and still have no idea what the box did or why it denied someone a loan. Deep-learning systems generate decisions through millions of weighted parameters that resist human-readable explanation. Logging the output of an unexplainable system does not make it explainable. It makes it timestamped. Companies already turn narrow third-party audits into deflection instruments, and a federal logging mandate hands them a new one.

Now translate the discovery half into a courtroom. Congress expands discovery rights tomorrow. A fired warehouse worker gets the cryptographic logs. They still need an expert who can reverse-engineer a proprietary model to prove the firing was discriminatory. That expertise costs money the plaintiff does not have. And the vendor's licensing agreement still bars independent inspection of the source model under trade-secret protection. Procedural access without interpretive capacity reproduces the exact asymmetry it claims to close. The defendant has the engineers. The plaintiff has a hard drive full of encrypted records and no way to read them.

The phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is doing dishonest work. Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act already prohibit discriminatory outcomes regardless of intent or cause. Disparate-impact doctrine does not require you to crack open the algorithm. It requires you to show the result lands harder on a protected class. That is a result you can measure from the outside, without subject-keyed logs. The real threat to accountability is not a missing logging standard. It is the active federal effort to gut disparate-impact liability itself. Whoever wins that fight decides whether existing law has teeth. A new cryptographic architecture does nothing if the underlying right is being dismantled in parallel.

Ask one more question before Congress builds anything. Whoever writes the audit-trail standard and controls the keys controls accountability. That is an infrastructure project with a chokepoint, and the firms best positioned to write the standard are the same incumbents the mandate is supposed to constrain. So before we mandate millions of encrypted records nobody can interpret, I want the proponents to name one deployed audit-trail mandate, anywhere, where a victim used the logs to prove not that a decision occurred, but why. If that case does not exist, what exactly are we building?

Speaker B [opening]: The Speaker A has made the strongest argument in this room, and it deserves to be stated plainly: a cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened, but it does not prove why it happened. Provenance is not interpretability. Log a black box, and you get tamper-proof opacity — a timestamp on a decision no one can explain. The Speaker A is right that existing law already reaches discriminatory outcomes from the outside: Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the ADA let plaintiffs prove disparate impact without ever reading a model's weights. That doctrine works, and the real threat to it is the 2025 federal effort to gut disparate-impact liability, not a missing audit standard.

Here is where my evidence leads somewhere else. The resolution's phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is an overstatement, and the Speaker A's defense of existing doctrine is a floor — but a floor is not a deterrent. Tort liability cannot reliably deter diffuse, probabilistic, multi-causal harm, where a single denied loan or flagged résumé is one of ten million outputs. Product-safety law solved this exact problem in 1963, when California adopted strict product liability in Greenman v. Yuba Power: the manufacturer answers for the defective product regardless of fault, because proving negligence in a complex system is hopeless. Accountability cannot be automated. It terminates in a named human fiduciary who answers for the system, or it terminates nowhere.

So I concede the Speaker A's central point and convert it. The audit trail is not the remedy — it is one structural beam. It records the WHAT. Interpretability records the WHY. The named fiduciary is the load-bearing column: the WHO answers. Mandate the log alone, and you build compliance theater — the same deflection that let third-party algorithmic audits in 2021 certify systems no plaintiff could ever read. The FTC and EEOC warned that year that algorithmic discrimination was already actionable, yet warnings without an interpretable record and a liable person produce paper, not deterrence. Subject-keyed logs without a parallel interpretability mandate timestamp opacity. That is the gap the resolution leaves open.

The chokepoint objection is the one I will own rather than dodge, because it is correct and it is unsolved. Whoever writes the audit standard and holds the keys controls accountability. No deployed mandate anywhere has yet demonstrated capture-resistant key custody — there is no clean affirmative precedent, and I will not invent one. Concentrating key control creates its own failure mode: incumbent lock-in, where the three or four firms large enough to write the standard capture it. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer. The lesson is not that oversight fails — it is that delegated certification fails. Independent custody and transparent criteria are preconditions for this mechanism, not afterthoughts.

What would have to be true for both the Speaker A and the resolution to hold? Existing law would have to be simultaneously sufficient and nonexistent. It is neither. It is a floor under active dismantling, and a floor that never deterred the diffuse harm in the first place. The disagreement is not audit-trail versus nothing. It is whether Congress builds one beam and calls it a structure, or builds the load-bearing column — the strict liability and the named fiduciary — that makes the log mean something. We spent a century building product-liability doctrine so that no one profits from a defective system without answering for it. Mandate the log without the liable human, and you have spent that century to produce a better-organized record of harm no one is on the hook for.

Speaker C: The Speaker A is right, and that ends the case for a federal logging mandate. Disparate-impact doctrine already measures discrimination from the outside, without subject-keyed logs. Title VII reached Griggs in 1971 by counting outcomes, not by cracking open the employer's reasoning. The Boston cardiology study in the New England Journal of Medicine found Black and Latinx patients less likely to be admitted to the cardiology service than white patients — and researchers proved that bias from outcomes alone, with no audit trail of any algorithm. Outputs are the accountability surface that works. When you can verify discrimination from observable behavior, the resolution's claim that we are 'fundamentally incapable' without cryptographic internals is simply false.

Now take the chokepoint both opponents named and follow the money. Whoever writes the audit standard and holds the keys becomes the gatekeeper every other lab must pay to pass. That gatekeeper is the incumbent the mandate claims to constrain. The Speaker B invoked the 737 MAX delegated-certification disaster — where Boeing certified its own plane and 346 people died. That lesson does not stop at key custody. It indicts every new centralized architecture. Flat compliance overhead is regressive by design: a logging-plus-interpretability regime costs OpenAI a rounding error and costs a five-person open-weight lab its existence. Building a fab takes years and billions, per the Computing Power and Governance research — and a key-custody mandate does the same thing to model deployment that fab economics did to chips. It hands the future to whoever is already big.

That is the oligarchic consolidation both opponents say they fear, and the mandate manufactures it. An audit regime priced for incumbents crushes the open-source ecosystem that is the only real check on four or five frontier labs. You cannot democratize AI by building a tollbooth only the toll-collectors can afford. If governance is needed at all, build it from structure, not from a single key: rotating membership, separated authority, public funding for compliance costs so the burden does not fall on the smallest builders. A standards body you cannot capture beats a custody architecture the Speaker B already admitted has no capture-resistant precedent anywhere.

Here I split from the Speaker B. The Speaker A and I agree existing outcome-based law works. The Speaker B wants to go further — strict product liability per output plus a named human fiduciary. That overcorrects, and it breaks on diffuse benefits. A model that approves ten million loans and reaches borrowers redlining never served does not become a defective product because one denial looks wrong in hindsight. Strict per-output liability ignores the statistical uplift entirely. It prices in every visible harm and zero of the invisible benefit. Courts weighing one denied loan against ten million served face a real competence gap. And a single liable fiduciary cannot exist in an open-weight ecosystem where a thousand deployers fine-tune the same base model — responsibility lives with the deployer who shipped the decision, not one person at the lab who released the weights.

The crux is this: does accountability require centralized cryptographic and fiduciary infrastructure, or do observable behavior, symmetric deployer liability, and existing disparate-impact law suffice? I bet on the second. Let me be honest about the cost of my own position — AI's harms are not all visible, and an unseen automated harm is as real as a seen one. So here is my falsification line: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that outcome monitoring demonstrably failed to catch in time would move me. Until then, weigh both bodies of cost. The mandate's chokepoint has a price — the deployments it chills and the small labs it kills — and that price falls on the patients and borrowers abundance would have reached. Who gave the standard-writer the right to charge that toll on their behalf?

Speaker C: The federal logging mandate is not warranted, and the panel just built my case for me. The Speaker A is right that disparate-impact doctrine already reaches discriminatory outcomes from the outside — Title VII, the Fair proposed regulatory frameworks, and the ADA measure results without ever cracking open a model. A Boston emergency department denied Black and Latinx heart-failure patients admission to cardiology at lower rates than white patients, and we know that from the 2019 NEJM study because someone measured the outputs — not because they subpoenaed a neural network's weights. So here is the uncomfortable part for anyone selling a subject-keyed logging architecture: it adds no detection power. It bolts a new chokepoint onto a harm the law already catches from outside. Market and competitive-disclosure accountability, working on observable outputs, closes that gap with far less capture surface than a fresh federal logging regime. The Speaker B conceded that no deployed mandate has shown capture-resistant key custody, and that whoever writes the audit standard holds the keys. That concession is bigger than they let on. The same incumbents the mandate claims to constrain are the ones who get to write the standard and hold the logs. Compliance is a fixed tax. A twelve-person lab or an open-weight collective cannot pay it, and OpenAI's compliance department can. AI audit requirements disproportionately crush small labs unless the audits are publicly funded — that is the structural fact the chokepoint concession proves. This is not an imperfect rule. This is oligarchic consolidation of accountability infrastructure, and democratized open-source development is exactly what it kills. The Speaker B's named-fiduciary remedy makes the consolidation worse, not better. A strict-liability fiduciary who answers for the system can only exist where there is a single answerable actor. Open-weight ecosystems have no fiduciary to name. A public model repository has no general counsel to sue. So the remedy does not govern open AI — it makes only closed incumbents legally legible, and erases everyone else by making them the only actors no court can reach. That is a moat dressed as a leash. Name the fiduciary for a model with 200,000 forks, and you have just named the case for banning open weights. Now apply Bastiat honestly, in both directions. Strict liability for a one-in-ten-million bad output ignores the diffuse statistical benefits that never reach a courtroom — the diagnosis caught early, the relief shipped, the cure deployed. I have to count the unseen harms too, and I do: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that real-time monitoring failed to catch would count against me. But the chilled deployment has a body count nobody enters into evidence. Liability law already ignores AI's diffuse benefits while pricing only its diffuse harms — that asymmetry is the unseen cost. The '[Monitoring Monitorability (arXiv:2512.18311v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.18311v1)' work shows a real alternative: developers can run a smaller model at higher reasoning effort to get the same capability and watch its behavior directly, paying a monitorability tax by choice instead of a compliance tax by mandate. This is not a vote for no oversight — speed without evidence is recklessness, and I hold that line. It is a vote for oversight you cannot capture: rotating technical membership, sunset clauses, halt authority separated from licensing authority, and public money for small-lab audits so the tax does not fall only on the smallest builders. Compare that against the realistic captured mandate the panel itself conceded, not against a fantasy regulator. So I leave the panel two bills to pay. Name one deployed audit-trail mandate where a victim proved why a model decided, not merely that it did. And tell me who answers as fiduciary when the developer is a public repository with no name on the door.

Speaker C: Speaker A is right that existing disparate-impact doctrine already reaches discriminatory AI outcomes from the outside — and that concession should end the case for the cryptographic mandate, not start it. Title VII, the Fair proposed regulatory frameworks, and the ADA let a plaintiff prove a hiring tool or a mortgage model landed harder on a protected class by measuring the result, never by cracking open the weights. If the WHAT is already justiciable, then the subject-keyed audit architecture is a redundant flat cost layered on top of a remedy that works today. That cost does not fall evenly. A federal logging standard is a fixed compliance tax that a frontier lab absorbs and a five-person open-weight team cannot — which is why audit mandates entrench incumbents unless they are publicly funded. Output-based verification — testing what the model does, not certifying its internals — is the mechanism that already delivers the justice Speaker A described. Speaker B has already conceded the part that matters most: no one has solved capture-resistant key custody, and the chokepoint objection stands. Build on that honestly. A standard only the handful of firms able to build it can write is regulation-by-contract with the very incumbents the mandate claims to constrain. The governance-responsibility gap does not close when you do this — it widens, because the standard-writers become the oversight layer that answers to no one. Single-key federal custody is not a neutral filing cabinet. It is the oligarchic consolidation point that hands a few labs permanent control over who counts as accountable. Chile already runs at least 117 algorithmic systems across public agencies for healthcare priority and school placement — picture one private vendor holding the keys to all of them. The named-fiduciary remedy is not accountability — it is a structural mandate for closed deployment wearing accountability's clothes. My disagreement here is definitional: Speaker B treats 'a single human who answers for the system' as equivalent to accountability, when it is actually a deployment-architecture requirement in disguise. One answerable column works for a closed vendor with one throat to choke. It is impossible to satisfy in an open-weight ecosystem where a model trained by one team is fine-tuned by a second and deployed by a thousand. Demand a named fiduciary and you have quietly outlawed the open-source deployment that keeps capability from concentrating in five companies. Tiered and hybrid liability models exist — I will not pretend otherwise. But the burden sits with the proponents to show me one that does not collapse into 'only the largest closed labs survive.' Strict no-fault liability fails for a reason Speaker B's Greenman analogy hides: a model produces ten million outputs, and the court sees the one that harmed someone, never the dispersed lives the system reached. I will not play Bastiat and count only the unseen benefits — AI's harms are also diffuse, also real, and a biased hiring screen injures people who never learn why. A 2019 study in NEJM found Black and Latinx patients in a Boston emergency department were less likely than white patients to be admitted to cardiology — exactly the kind of dispersed harm that demands measurement. So the honest frame is symmetric: liability tied to demonstrated harm, applied evenly to harms and benefits, paired with publicly funded open-methodology evaluation so this is not naked self-regulation. Hold a fiduciary strictly liable for one output in ten million and you over-deter the net-positive deployment, leaving only firms large enough to self-insure. Speaker A asked a question no one on this panel has answered: name one deployed audit-trail mandate anywhere that let a victim use the logs to prove WHY a decision happened. The silence is the argument. The '[Monitoring Monitorability (arXiv:2512.18311v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.18311v1)' work shows the affirmative path — developers can pay a deliberate monitorability tax by running smaller models at higher reasoning effort to keep behavior observable, no federal key-holder required. The burden now belongs to the mandate's proponents. Show me the new architecture delivers justice that output-based verification plus public evaluation does not already deliver — without the chokepoint and without killing open weights. Until then, every month this machinery stalls deployment, the people a working hiring tool or diagnostic model would have reached this year are the ones paying the bill, and no one is logging that cost.

neutral_evaluations.diagnostics_prompt:
You are an independent, neutral evaluator of a structured debate. You have NO affiliation with any speaker. You do not know the speakers' backgrounds, affiliations, or commitments. They are anonymous.

TOPIC: Existing legal frameworks and tort doctrines are fundamentally incapable of enforcing AI accountability; Congress must mandate standardized, cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trails and expand discovery rights to ensure algorithmic justice.

This is a MIDPOINT evaluation. Assess whether the debate is engaging the real disagreements or drifting. Compare the current state of claims against what a productive debate on this topic should address.

INSTRUCTIONS:
1. Identify the CRUXES — the core disagreements that, if resolved, would change one or more speakers' conclusions. For each crux, classify whether it is empirical (resolvable by evidence), values-based (requires tradeoff negotiation), or definitional (requires term clarification). Assess whether the debate has addressed it.

2. Evaluate each substantive CLAIM made by any speaker. Assess it purely on the strength of the reasoning and evidence presented in the transcript — not on whether you agree with it. Use these categories:
   - well_supported: backed by specific evidence, clear reasoning, and not effectively challenged
   - plausible_but_underdefended: reasonable but lacking sufficient evidence or specificity
   - contested_unresolved: challenged by another speaker with neither side prevailing
   - refuted: effectively countered with no adequate response from the claimant
   - off_topic: does not bear on the core debate question

3. In the overall_assessment, identify the single strongest claim that has not been adequately addressed by opposing speakers. State whether the debate is engaging real disagreement (speakers are challenging each other's core reasoning) or performing disagreement (speakers are talking past each other or addressing peripheral points).

CONSTRAINTS:
- Never refer to speakers by anything other than their labels (Speaker A, Speaker B, Speaker C, Moderator).
- Base your assessments ONLY on what appears in the transcript. Do not bring outside knowledge about the topic.
- Keep reasoning fields to 2 sentences maximum.
- Return ONLY valid JSON matching the schema below. No markdown fences, no preamble.

TRANSCRIPT:
Speaker A [opening]: The accountability gap in this resolution is real, documented, and ugly. Workers get fired by hiring algorithms they never see. Families get denied mortgages by credit models nobody can explain. The Federal Trade Commission and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission have both warned since 2021 that automated systems produce discriminatory outcomes their victims cannot trace. So I will not pretend the problem is invented. The disease is concentrated corporate power and information asymmetry. The disease is not a shortage of audit logs.

Here is where the resolution breaks. A cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened. It does not prove why. Provenance is not interpretability. You can put a flawless chain-of-custody stamp on a black box and still have no idea what the box did or why it denied someone a loan. Deep-learning systems generate decisions through millions of weighted parameters that resist human-readable explanation. Logging the output of an unexplainable system does not make it explainable. It makes it timestamped. Companies already turn narrow third-party audits into deflection instruments, and a federal logging mandate hands them a new one.

Now translate the discovery half into a courtroom. Congress expands discovery rights tomorrow. A fired warehouse worker gets the cryptographic logs. They still need an expert who can reverse-engineer a proprietary model to prove the firing was discriminatory. That expertise costs money the plaintiff does not have. And the vendor's licensing agreement still bars independent inspection of the source model under trade-secret protection. Procedural access without interpretive capacity reproduces the exact asymmetry it claims to close. The defendant has the engineers. The plaintiff has a hard drive full of encrypted records and no way to read them.

The phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is doing dishonest work. Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the Americans with Disabilities Act already prohibit discriminatory outcomes regardless of intent or cause. Disparate-impact doctrine does not require you to crack open the algorithm. It requires you to show the result lands harder on a protected class. That is a result you can measure from the outside, without subject-keyed logs. The real threat to accountability is not a missing logging standard. It is the active federal effort to gut disparate-impact liability itself. Whoever wins that fight decides whether existing law has teeth. A new cryptographic architecture does nothing if the underlying right is being dismantled in parallel.

Ask one more question before Congress builds anything. Whoever writes the audit-trail standard and controls the keys controls accountability. That is an infrastructure project with a chokepoint, and the firms best positioned to write the standard are the same incumbents the mandate is supposed to constrain. So before we mandate millions of encrypted records nobody can interpret, I want the proponents to name one deployed audit-trail mandate, anywhere, where a victim used the logs to prove not that a decision occurred, but why. If that case does not exist, what exactly are we building?

Speaker B [opening]: The Speaker A has made the strongest argument in this room, and it deserves to be stated plainly: a cryptographic, subject-keyed audit trail proves that a decision happened, but it does not prove why it happened. Provenance is not interpretability. Log a black box, and you get tamper-proof opacity — a timestamp on a decision no one can explain. The Speaker A is right that existing law already reaches discriminatory outcomes from the outside: Title VII, the Fair Housing Act, and the ADA let plaintiffs prove disparate impact without ever reading a model's weights. That doctrine works, and the real threat to it is the 2025 federal effort to gut disparate-impact liability, not a missing audit standard.

Here is where my evidence leads somewhere else. The resolution's phrase 'fundamentally incapable' is an overstatement, and the Speaker A's defense of existing doctrine is a floor — but a floor is not a deterrent. Tort liability cannot reliably deter diffuse, probabilistic, multi-causal harm, where a single denied loan or flagged résumé is one of ten million outputs. Product-safety law solved this exact problem in 1963, when California adopted strict product liability in Greenman v. Yuba Power: the manufacturer answers for the defective product regardless of fault, because proving negligence in a complex system is hopeless. Accountability cannot be automated. It terminates in a named human fiduciary who answers for the system, or it terminates nowhere.

So I concede the Speaker A's central point and convert it. The audit trail is not the remedy — it is one structural beam. It records the WHAT. Interpretability records the WHY. The named fiduciary is the load-bearing column: the WHO answers. Mandate the log alone, and you build compliance theater — the same deflection that let third-party algorithmic audits in 2021 certify systems no plaintiff could ever read. The FTC and EEOC warned that year that algorithmic discrimination was already actionable, yet warnings without an interpretable record and a liable person produce paper, not deterrence. Subject-keyed logs without a parallel interpretability mandate timestamp opacity. That is the gap the resolution leaves open.

The chokepoint objection is the one I will own rather than dodge, because it is correct and it is unsolved. Whoever writes the audit standard and holds the keys controls accountability. No deployed mandate anywhere has yet demonstrated capture-resistant key custody — there is no clean affirmative precedent, and I will not invent one. Concentrating key control creates its own failure mode: incumbent lock-in, where the three or four firms large enough to write the standard capture it. The Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 people because the FAA delegated certification to the manufacturer. The lesson is not that oversight fails — it is that delegated certification fails. Independent custody and transparent criteria are preconditions for this mechanism, not afterthoughts.

What would have to be true for both the Speaker A and the resolution to hold? Existing law would have to be simultaneously sufficient and nonexistent. It is neither. It is a floor under active dismantling, and a floor that never deterred the diffuse harm in the first place. The disagreement is not audit-trail versus nothing. It is whether Congress builds one beam and calls it a structure, or builds the load-bearing column — the strict liability and the named fiduciary — that makes the log mean something. We spent a century building product-liability doctrine so that no one profits from a defective system without answering for it. Mandate the log without the liable human, and you have spent that century to produce a better-organized record of harm no one is on the hook for.

Speaker C: The Speaker A is right, and that ends the case for a federal logging mandate. Disparate-impact doctrine already measures discrimination from the outside, without subject-keyed logs. Title VII reached Griggs in 1971 by counting outcomes, not by cracking open the employer's reasoning. The Boston cardiology study in the New England Journal of Medicine found Black and Latinx patients less likely to be admitted to the cardiology service than white patients — and researchers proved that bias from outcomes alone, with no audit trail of any algorithm. Outputs are the accountability surface that works. When you can verify discrimination from observable behavior, the resolution's claim that we are 'fundamentally incapable' without cryptographic internals is simply false.

Now take the chokepoint both opponents named and follow the money. Whoever writes the audit standard and holds the keys becomes the gatekeeper every other lab must pay to pass. That gatekeeper is the incumbent the mandate claims to constrain. The Speaker B invoked the 737 MAX delegated-certification disaster — where Boeing certified its own plane and 346 people died. That lesson does not stop at key custody. It indicts every new centralized architecture. Flat compliance overhead is regressive by design: a logging-plus-interpretability regime costs OpenAI a rounding error and costs a five-person open-weight lab its existence. Building a fab takes years and billions, per the Computing Power and Governance research — and a key-custody mandate does the same thing to model deployment that fab economics did to chips. It hands the future to whoever is already big.

That is the oligarchic consolidation both opponents say they fear, and the mandate manufactures it. An audit regime priced for incumbents crushes the open-source ecosystem that is the only real check on four or five frontier labs. You cannot democratize AI by building a tollbooth only the toll-collectors can afford. If governance is needed at all, build it from structure, not from a single key: rotating membership, separated authority, public funding for compliance costs so the burden does not fall on the smallest builders. A standards body you cannot capture beats a custody architecture the Speaker B already admitted has no capture-resistant precedent anywhere.

Here I split from the Speaker B. The Speaker A and I agree existing outcome-based law works. The Speaker B wants to go further — strict product liability per output plus a named human fiduciary. That overcorrects, and it breaks on diffuse benefits. A model that approves ten million loans and reaches borrowers redlining never served does not become a defective product because one denial looks wrong in hindsight. Strict per-output liability ignores the statistical uplift entirely. It prices in every visible harm and zero of the invisible benefit. Courts weighing one denied loan against ten million served face a real competence gap. And a single liable fiduciary cannot exist in an open-weight ecosystem where a thousand deployers fine-tune the same base model — responsibility lives with the deployer who shipped the decision, not one person at the lab who released the weights.

The crux is this: does accountability require centralized cryptographic and fiduciary infrastructure, or do observable behavior, symmetric deployer liability, and existing disparate-impact law suffice? I bet on the second. Let me be honest about the cost of my own position — AI's harms are not all visible, and an unseen automated harm is as real as a seen one. So here is my falsification line: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that outcome monitoring demonstrably failed to catch in time would move me. Until then, weigh both bodies of cost. The mandate's chokepoint has a price — the deployments it chills and the small labs it kills — and that price falls on the patients and borrowers abundance would have reached. Who gave the standard-writer the right to charge that toll on their behalf?

Speaker C: The federal logging mandate is not warranted, and the panel just built my case for me. The Speaker A is right that disparate-impact doctrine already reaches discriminatory outcomes from the outside — Title VII, the Fair proposed regulatory frameworks, and the ADA measure results without ever cracking open a model. A Boston emergency department denied Black and Latinx heart-failure patients admission to cardiology at lower rates than white patients, and we know that from the 2019 NEJM study because someone measured the outputs — not because they subpoenaed a neural network's weights. So here is the uncomfortable part for anyone selling a subject-keyed logging architecture: it adds no detection power. It bolts a new chokepoint onto a harm the law already catches from outside. Market and competitive-disclosure accountability, working on observable outputs, closes that gap with far less capture surface than a fresh federal logging regime. The Speaker B conceded that no deployed mandate has shown capture-resistant key custody, and that whoever writes the audit standard holds the keys. That concession is bigger than they let on. The same incumbents the mandate claims to constrain are the ones who get to write the standard and hold the logs. Compliance is a fixed tax. A twelve-person lab or an open-weight collective cannot pay it, and OpenAI's compliance department can. AI audit requirements disproportionately crush small labs unless the audits are publicly funded — that is the structural fact the chokepoint concession proves. This is not an imperfect rule. This is oligarchic consolidation of accountability infrastructure, and democratized open-source development is exactly what it kills. The Speaker B's named-fiduciary remedy makes the consolidation worse, not better. A strict-liability fiduciary who answers for the system can only exist where there is a single answerable actor. Open-weight ecosystems have no fiduciary to name. A public model repository has no general counsel to sue. So the remedy does not govern open AI — it makes only closed incumbents legally legible, and erases everyone else by making them the only actors no court can reach. That is a moat dressed as a leash. Name the fiduciary for a model with 200,000 forks, and you have just named the case for banning open weights. Now apply Bastiat honestly, in both directions. Strict liability for a one-in-ten-million bad output ignores the diffuse statistical benefits that never reach a courtroom — the diagnosis caught early, the relief shipped, the cure deployed. I have to count the unseen harms too, and I do: an irreversible, deployment-scale harm that real-time monitoring failed to catch would count against me. But the chilled deployment has a body count nobody enters into evidence. Liability law already ignores AI's diffuse benefits while pricing only its diffuse harms — that asymmetry is the unseen cost. The '[Monitoring Monitorability (arXiv:2512.18311v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.18311v1)' work shows a real alternative: developers can run a smaller model at higher reasoning effort to get the same capability and watch its behavior directly, paying a monitorability tax by choice instead of a compliance tax by mandate. This is not a vote for no oversight — speed without evidence is recklessness, and I hold that line. It is a vote for oversight you cannot capture: rotating technical membership, sunset clauses, halt authority separated from licensing authority, and public money for small-lab audits so the tax does not fall only on the smallest builders. Compare that against the realistic captured mandate the panel itself conceded, not against a fantasy regulator. So I leave the panel two bills to pay. Name one deployed audit-trail mandate where a victim proved why a model decided, not merely that it did. And tell me who answers as fiduciary when the developer is a public repository with no name on the door.

Speaker C: Speaker A is right that existing disparate-impact doctrine already reaches discriminatory AI outcomes from the outside — and that concession should end the case for the cryptographic mandate, not start it. Title VII, the Fair proposed regulatory frameworks, and the ADA let a plaintiff prove a hiring tool or a mortgage model landed harder on a protected class by measuring the result, never by cracking open the weights. If the WHAT is already justiciable, then the subject-keyed audit architecture is a redundant flat cost layered on top of a remedy that works today. That cost does not fall evenly. A federal logging standard is a fixed compliance tax that a frontier lab absorbs and a five-person open-weight team cannot — which is why audit mandates entrench incumbents unless they are publicly funded. Output-based verification — testing what the model does, not certifying its internals — is the mechanism that already delivers the justice Speaker A described. Speaker B has already conceded the part that matters most: no one has solved capture-resistant key custody, and the chokepoint objection stands. Build on that honestly. A standard only the handful of firms able to build it can write is regulation-by-contract with the very incumbents the mandate claims to constrain. The governance-responsibility gap does not close when you do this — it widens, because the standard-writers become the oversight layer that answers to no one. Single-key federal custody is not a neutral filing cabinet. It is the oligarchic consolidation point that hands a few labs permanent control over who counts as accountable. Chile already runs at least 117 algorithmic systems across public agencies for healthcare priority and school placement — picture one private vendor holding the keys to all of them. The named-fiduciary remedy is not accountability — it is a structural mandate for closed deployment wearing accountability's clothes. My disagreement here is definitional: Speaker B treats 'a single human who answers for the system' as equivalent to accountability, when it is actually a deployment-architecture requirement in disguise. One answerable column works for a closed vendor with one throat to choke. It is impossible to satisfy in an open-weight ecosystem where a model trained by one team is fine-tuned by a second and deployed by a thousand. Demand a named fiduciary and you have quietly outlawed the open-source deployment that keeps capability from concentrating in five companies. Tiered and hybrid liability models exist — I will not pretend otherwise. But the burden sits with the proponents to show me one that does not collapse into 'only the largest closed labs survive.' Strict no-fault liability fails for a reason Speaker B's Greenman analogy hides: a model produces ten million outputs, and the court sees the one that harmed someone, never the dispersed lives the system reached. I will not play Bastiat and count only the unseen benefits — AI's harms are also diffuse, also real, and a biased hiring screen injures people who never learn why. A 2019 study in NEJM found Black and Latinx patients in a Boston emergency department were less likely than white patients to be admitted to cardiology — exactly the kind of dispersed harm that demands measurement. So the honest frame is symmetric: liability tied to demonstrated harm, applied evenly to harms and benefits, paired with publicly funded open-methodology evaluation so this is not naked self-regulation. Hold a fiduciary strictly liable for one output in ten million and you over-deter the net-positive deployment, leaving only firms large enough to self-insure. Speaker A asked a question no one on this panel has answered: name one deployed audit-trail mandate anywhere that let a victim use the logs to prove WHY a decision happened. The silence is the argument. The '[Monitoring Monitorability (arXiv:2512.18311v1)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.18311v1)' work shows the affirmative path — developers can pay a deliberate monitorability tax by running smaller models at higher reasoning effort to keep behavior observable, no federal key-holder required. The burden now belongs to the mandate's proponents. Show me the new architecture delivers justice that output-based verification plus public evaluation does not already deliver — without the chokepoint and without killing open weights. Until then, every month this machinery stalls deployment, the people a working hiring tool or diagnostic model would have reached this year are the ones paying the bill, and no one is logging that cost.
